newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-FORMER HEAVYWEIGHT CHAMP MCCALL SENT TO MENTAL HOSPITAL.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-FORMER HEAVYWEIGHT CHAMP MCCALL SENT TO MENTAL HOSPITAL.

text.p: Former heavyweight champion Oliver McCall, who broke down in tears and was disqualified in a title fight in February, was sent to a mental hospital on a court order obtained by his wife and mother, police said Wednesday.

The Martinsville, Virginia, police said they picked up McCall last Saturday night and took him to the Southern Virginia Mental Health Institute in nearby Danville, where he was admitted after a health officer testified that he was mentally ill.
Martinsville police Corporal K.L. Gooding said he picked up McCall after his wife and mother had been issued an emergency custody order, saying "they were afraid for his well-being."
McCall, whom police said had been remodeling a restaurant in Martinsville, offered no resistence when they stopped him while he was walking on a street.
"He came willingly and peacefully," said Corporal K.L. Gooding. "He gave nobody no trouble. We've never had any trouble with him."
Gooding said McCall, who lives in nearby Collinsville, was still in the hospital as of Tuesday night. A hospital spokeswoman said she could not release information about a patient.

McCall, 31, seemed to be having a nervous breakdown in the ring against Briton Lennox Lewis last February 7, when he simply stopped fighting in their bout for the vacant World Boxing Council heavyweight title in Las Vegas.

Referee Mills Lane, after asking McCall between the third and fourth rounds if he wanted to continue fighting, stepped in and waved the fight off in the fifth round. McCall had been walking away from Lewis, often with his back turned to him, refusing to fight and offering little resistence when Lewis went after him.
McCall, 31, "seemed to want to get knocked out," Lane said after the fight.
The Nevada State Athletic Commission withheld McCall's $3,075,500 purse, pending a hearing set for April 26 to hear the fighter's side of his behaviour in the ring against Lewis.
The maximum the commission can fine a fighter is $250,000, the Commission's Executive Director Marc Ratner said.
